scenarios.title: Modular personal agents combine small local models instead of renting giant central clouds
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Rather than paying recurring subscriptions to central cloud vendors who monitor query logs, people run compact, private agent runtimes on their laptops and phones. Using descent-aligned routing, their personal agents dynamically assemble specialized micro-experts for bookkeeping, contract drafting, and private communication without transmitting raw personal data over the network.
scenarios.premise: Recent research in combinatorial expert routing demonstrates that scoring gradient descent alignment allows compact 3B-parameter models to dynamically compose low-rank adapters, matching monolithic model capabilities while requiring under half the parameter overhead.
scenarios.how: The network develops open specifications for modular model routing, verifies privacy-preserving on-device adapters, and coordinates shared benchmarks that help open-source runtimes run efficiently on affordable consumer hardware.

outcomes.name: Centralized model providers restrict local model execution
outcomes.description: Frontier cloud corporations lobby for mandatory cryptographic signatures on model weights, restricting the ability of consumer hardware to run independent local adapters.
outcomes.example: A laptop manufacturer deploys a firmware update blocking unsigned neural network weights, preventing an independent researcher in Berlin from running private personal adapters.

outcomes.name: Open-weight combinatorial ecosystems displace subscription clouds
outcomes.description: Open-weight developer communities share verified, modular skill adapters that personal agents combine on the fly, making private local inference the standard for personal computing.
outcomes.example: An independent accountant in Montreal processes confidential client financial audits using local adapters on a desktop computer with no outbound network dependencies.

outcomes.name: Specialized silicon pricing keeps advanced local routing inaccessible to low-income users
outcomes.description: Hardware vendors maintain premium pricing on high-bandwidth unified memory architectures, restricting fluid local combinatorial routing to affluent households while lower-income users remain on subsidized ad-supported clouds.
outcomes.example: A student in Manila is forced to use an ad-supported cloud assistant because affordable laptops lack sufficient unified memory bandwidth to switch between complex local adapters.

scenarios.title: AI planning tools trained on revised history fail when real crises hit
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Regional hospital systems and municipal budget offices rely heavily on automated predictive suites to allocate emergency staff and supplies. Because vendors trained these systems on cleansed retrospective registries where initial reporting errors had been retroactively corrected, the tools routinely underestimate volatility during fast-moving crises, leading to severe under-staffing during seasonal illness spikes.
scenarios.premise: Predictive models evaluated on historical backtests often look superhuman because retrospective databases quietly incorporate revisions made months after events occurred. In live operations, models must forecast from unrevised, noisy real-time numbers, causing apparent forecasting superiority to evaporate when unexpected disruptions happen.
scenarios.how: The network publishes open, point-in-time forecasting evaluations that expose data revision leakage, provides synthetic stress-testing datasets reflecting real-time reporting delays, and equips community analysts with verification tools to audit commercial predictive claims.

outcomes.name: Silent planning failures during seasonal surges
outcomes.description: Public agencies trust automated forecasts and cut buffer capacities, only to suffer severe resource shortfalls when real-time reporting lags mask incoming demand.
outcomes.example: A county health department cuts emergency staffing contracts by 25% based on an AI forecast, then faces an ICU bed crisis when pediatric admissions spike faster than unrevised clinic feeds indicate.

outcomes.name: Standardized point-in-time evaluation registries
outcomes.description: Institutions adopt immutable, point-in-time evaluation benchmarks that evaluate models only on the exact data vintages available at decision time.
outcomes.example: A public health consortium mandates that healthcare forecasting agents demonstrate calibrated coverage against historical snapshots before qualifying for municipal procurement.

outcomes.name: Proprietary simulation sandboxes entrench commercial forecasting monopolies
outcomes.description: Large cloud providers offer synthetic closed-world simulation suites that benchmark models on proprietary data, shutting out open public audit while charging high subscription fees.
outcomes.example: A major enterprise cloud vendor packages an annual certified predictive assurance subscription that healthcare networks buy to satisfy procurement mandates without opening models to external scrutiny.

scenarios.title: Everyday computers run full-sized personal AI assistants without cloud subscriptions
scenarios.world: It is 2028. Millions of people run their own primary assistant on an inexpensive desktop computer or repurposed workstation. Because their model runs on local silicon, personal emails, medical records, and family financial accounts never leave the physical device. Instead of renting cloud agents that sell conversational insights to advertisers, individuals rely on open local engines that answer queries in fractions of a second.
scenarios.premise: Memory management hacks and split storage prefilling allow common consumer graphics cards to run capable 27-billion parameter language models locally. This makes private personal assistants practical on home computers without recurring server fees.
scenarios.how: The network provides open reference designs for personal twins that run inside standard web browsers and local runtimes, demonstrating that private models can deliver daily value without cloud surveillance.

outcomes.name: Proprietary clouds lock down device drivers to preserve subscription revenue
outcomes.description: Commercial operating systems restrict unapproved local model runtimes, nudging consumers back toward paid cloud subscriptions with automated security warnings.
outcomes.example: A home user sees their local model blocked by an operating system update that requires all agent software to use remote cloud verification.

outcomes.name: Independent communities establish shared local-first assistant runtimes
outcomes.description: Open developer cooperatives maintain lightweight, hardware-tuned assistant runtimes that run smoothly across consumer hardware without central servers.
outcomes.example: A municipal credit union distributes a local twin profile that helps 12,000 residents manage household debt without sending financial data over the internet.

outcomes.name: Hardware manufacturers focus memory bandwidth on server clusters
outcomes.description: Global memory chip makers prioritize multi-terabyte data center modules over consumer cards, keeping retail consumer GPU memory bus widths narrow.
outcomes.example: A consumer building a home assistant finds mid-range retail graphics cards remain capped at 16 gigabytes of video memory, forcing larger models to offload to storage.

scenarios.title: Worker cooperatives struggle to share out tasks fairly once groups grow past four people
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Freelancer collectives, community care cooperatives, and decentralized research groups attempt to run without bosses by using automated peer-matching software to allocate client projects and shift tasks. In small teams of three or four participants, members find the assignments mutually agreeable and collaborative morale remains high. However, as soon as a cooperative expands its membership past four active participants, sequential task assignment inevitably produces perceived disparities: certain members repeatedly receive undesirable shifts while others get preferred tasks. Without central executive discretion to reassign work or arbitrary subsidy pools to smooth grievances, cooperatives experience bitter factional disputes, with some members calling for traditional hierarchical managers and others abandoning the collective entirely.
scenarios.premise: Mathematical proofs establish that online allocation algorithms cannot maintain positive envy-freeness up to one item for teams of five or more people without central subsidy pools. As decentralized worker cooperatives attempt to allocate dynamic workloads purely peer-to-peer, groups larger than four members face severe perceived unfairness.
scenarios.how: By developing open simulation models and operational blueprints, the network provides cooperative associations with verifiable architectures for polycentric circles. Instead of attempting brittle global dispatch across dozens of people, cooperatives can implement bounded four-person working units coupled with privacy-preserving mutual credit clearing, demonstrating in simulation how peer coordination remains fair without central executives.

outcomes.name: Cooperatives re-introduce hierarchical managerial bosses
outcomes.description: Unable to resolve perceived unfairness mathematically in larger teams, growing cooperatives abandon pure peer allocation and hire traditional managers to assign tasks by decree.
outcomes.example: A twelve-person home health care cooperative in Montreal votes to hire an operations manager after peer dispatch leaves two nurses feeling consistently stuck with difficult weekend shifts.

outcomes.name: Teams adopt bounded four-person circles with peer credit clearing
outcomes.description: Cooperatives reorganize into small, mathematically bounded operational circles of four people, using mutual credit rebalancing across circles to maintain overall balance.
outcomes.example: A software development association divides a forty-person engineering group into ten four-person pods that clear tasks internally, settling cross-pod imbalances via monthly contribution credits.

outcomes.name: External labor platforms absorb frustrated cooperative members
outcomes.description: Disillusioned by persistent scheduling conflicts in flat cooperatives, skilled workers leave for proprietary algorithmic gig platforms that offer predictable piece-rate pay despite high platform fees.
outcomes.example: Four freelance translation collectives dissolve after scheduling disputes, and their members migrate to commercial delivery portals.

scenarios.title: Governments offer broad copyright waivers to lure AI companies, leaving local creators uncompensated
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Several mid-sized nations have established regulatory safe harbors where commercial AI crawlers can scrape local media, books, scientific archives, and artistic works without license fees or consent. Major technology firms route their continuous training pipelines through cloud clusters located in these safe harbors. Independent writers and recording artists find their styles and outputs reproduced on commercial platforms while their traditional licensing royalties drop to zero. In response, creative guilds establish decentralized provenance registries that cryptographically sign source works and enforce mutual-credit licensing outside conventional copyright treaties.
scenarios.premise: National governments compete for corporate artificial intelligence investment by carving out sweeping copyright exemptions for model training. This allows frontier model developers to ingest creative work across jurisdictions without compensating local authors, musicians, and independent researchers.
scenarios.how: Decentralized value accounting and cooperative member-owned registries replace statutory waivers with transparent, direct attribution. When creative communities hold their own records and license through verified personal agent networks, corporate platforms cannot rely on geographic legal loopholes to extract value without reciprocity.

outcomes.name: Global training arbitrage wipes out local creator livelihoods
outcomes.description: Tech conglomerates route model training to jurisdictions with statutory scraping waivers, bypassing bilateral licensing and leaving independent creators without revenue.
outcomes.example: An Australian scriptwriter discovers a commercial streaming assistant generating full series episodes in their signature voice after their produced teleplays were scraped legally in an offshore data haven.

outcomes.name: Creator cooperatives deploy verifiable provenance registries
outcomes.description: Writers, musicians, and visual artists form autonomous cooperatives that publish cryptographic content manifests, requiring personal agents and honest models to settle micro-licensing directly.
outcomes.example: A union of 15,000 independent illustrators registers daily artwork with signed attribution receipts, and ethical agent runtimes automatically negotiate micropayments before including their portfolios in style fine-tuning.

outcomes.name: Legacy publishers retreat behind private subscription firewalls
outcomes.description: Major publishing conglomerates respond to government scraping waivers by locking all archives and new publications behind proprietary enterprise paywalls, restricting public knowledge access regardless of grassroots attribution alternatives.
outcomes.example: A scientific publishing syndicate removes all open-access journals and public abstracts, requiring individual reader subscriptions and proprietary hardware readers to prevent offshore AI harvesting.

scenarios.title: Tech platforms push closed agent networks that charge commissions on everyday deals
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Millions of households use platform-provided digital assistants to manage household shopping, medical appointments, and freelance contracts. Rather than browsing websites or sending emails directly, people tell their assistant what they need, and corporate agent networks negotiate directly with vendor agents. When an independent graphic designer looks for client work, platform agents match them with small business buyers but silently deduct a 15 percent routing fee while keeping the communication logs inside proprietary cloud silos.
scenarios.premise: Major technology firms are launching consumer agent networks designed to have corporate AI assistants negotiate shopping, scheduling, and freelance work with each other. Because these platforms mediate both sides of the conversation, they control the interaction history, monitor personal preferences, and introduce proprietary tollgates on every concluded transaction.
scenarios.how: The collective intelligence network develops and distributes open-source personal twin runtimes that execute on local devices. By providing client-side cryptographic delegation, verifiable local execution receipts, and decentralized peer-to-peer negotiation protocols, the network enables individuals to transact directly with other people's agents without submitting their data or earnings to centralized platforms.

outcomes.name: Proprietary agent walled gardens capture consumer commerce
outcomes.description: Two or three dominant tech platforms operate closed agent networks that take unilateral commission fees on automated transactions and hide actual price discovery from consumers.
outcomes.example: A freelance translator's assistant is barred from bidding on corporate translation jobs unless their account routes all milestone escrow payments through the platform's closed assistant network.

outcomes.name: Hardware makers restrict background execution to certified agents
outcomes.description: Smartphone and laptop operating system vendors restrict persistent low-power background processing to their own certified commercial assistants, preventing open alternative agents from running continuously on consumer devices.
outcomes.example: A smartphone manufacturer updates its firmware to terminate any uncertified background agent after three minutes of screen inactivity, leaving users unable to host their own persistent autonomous twins regardless of open software availability.

outcomes.name: Open peer-to-peer twins establish direct negotiation channels
outcomes.description: Workers and consumers run local open-weight twins on personal devices that communicate over open standards, exchanging signed credentials and direct payments without platform intermediaries.
outcomes.example: A group of independent electricians uses open personal twins to negotiate neighborhood service contracts directly with homeowners' local assistants, settling payments instantly with cryptographic receipts and zero platform fees.
